title: Tea: From Leaf to Cup
intro: You should spend about 20 minutes on this passage.

paras.t: Tea is the most widely drunk beverage in the world after water. According to legend, it was discovered in China around 2737 BC, when leaves from a wild tree blew into a pot of water that the emperor Shennong was boiling. Whatever the truth of the story, Chinese people were certainly drinking tea more than two thousand years ago, at first as a medicine and later for pleasure. By the Tang dynasty, in the eighth century, tea had become so popular that a scholar named Lu Yu wrote the first known book about it, describing how to grow, prepare and serve the drink.

Tea comes from a single plant, Camellia sinensis, an evergreen bush that grows best in warm, wet climates on hillsides. The young leaves and buds are picked by hand, and the best tea comes from the top two leaves and the bud. A skilled worker can pick about twenty kilograms of leaves in a day, but it takes around four kilograms of fresh leaf to make one kilogram of dry tea. Because the work is so careful, tea-picking has traditionally been done mainly by women, who learn the skill from their mothers and grandmothers.

The difference between types of tea lies in how the leaves are treated after picking. For green tea, the leaves are heated quickly to stop them from changing colour, and then dried. For black tea, the leaves are rolled and left to oxidise, which turns them dark and gives a stronger flavour. Oolong tea is partly oxidised, so its taste lies between the two. White tea is the least treated: the young buds are simply dried in the air. Each type must be brewed differently: green and white teas need cooler water, while black tea is best made with water that has just boiled.

Tea reached Europe in the early seventeenth century, carried by Dutch and Portuguese traders. At first it was so expensive that only the rich could afford it. By the eighteenth century, however, Britain was importing huge quantities, and a heavy tax led to widespread smuggling. Later, the British began to grow tea in India and Sri Lanka, because they wanted a supply that did not depend on China. Today, afternoon tea with sandwiches and cakes is still seen as a typical British custom, although most people now drink their tea from a simple bag.

In Central Asia, tea has always played a social role. In Uzbekistan, a host who pours tea for a guest shows respect by filling the cup only part of the way. The guest's cup is refilled often, so that the tea stays hot, and a full cup is sometimes taken as a sign that the host would like the guest to leave. Visitors to a home are often offered tea before anything else, and refusing it may seem impolite. Tea is usually served in a teahouse, or choyxona, together with bread, sweets and dried fruit.

Tea has long been linked with good health. Researchers have found that tea contains antioxidants, substances that may protect cells from damage, and that moderate drinking is unlikely to cause harm. However, the claims made for tea are sometimes exaggerated. Dr Yuki Tanaka, a nutrition scientist, notes that the strongest evidence comes from studies of people who drink tea, which cannot prove that tea alone is the cause of their good health.

Today, tea is a major industry. India and China together produce more than half of the world's tea, and Kenya is the largest exporter of black tea. Climate change is a growing worry for growers, because rising temperatures and changing rainfall affect both the quantity and the flavour of the leaves. Some farms have started to plant at higher altitudes, where the air is cooler, while others are testing new varieties that tolerate heat.
